title: Chocolate Aromas Boost Workout Reps Without Extra Effort
summary:
What if the secret to a better workout was waiting in your candy bar? A new study published in Frontiers in Physiology suggests that simply smelling chocolate could help you push through resistance training with less perceived effort.

Researchers at the University of Malaya tested 23 moderately trained men in their early to mid-20s. The men fasted for at least 10 hours, then performed leg extensions — an exercise where you sit and straighten your legs against resistance. Before and between sets, they were exposed to one of three scents: liquified dark chocolate (90% cocoa), liquified milk chocolate (60% cocoa), or water as a control.

The results were surprising. Both chocolate scents increased the total number of repetitions the men could complete, but they didn't feel like they were working any harder. "Seeing a substantial increase in repetitions without the athletes feeling like they were exerting themselves any harder is a fascinating psychobiological outcome," said senior author Dr. Mohamed Nashrudin bin Naharudin.

The two chocolates had different effects on appetite. Dark chocolate was linked to lower hunger and greater fullness before exercise. Milk chocolate, on the other hand, was rated as more pleasant but didn't change hunger levels. The researchers think this is because of learned associations: dark chocolate signals a rich, filling food, tricking the body into an anticipatory state of fullness. Milk chocolate acts more like a reward cue, making the workout environment more enjoyable.

However, the study has limitations. The researchers didn't measure blood hormones or brain activity, so they can't explain exactly how the smells caused these changes. The biological explanation remains speculative. Also, the sample was small — only 23 men — and all were moderately trained, so the results might not apply to everyone.

Still, the findings open up intriguing possibilities about how our sense of smell can influence both appetite and physical performance. Could smelling certain foods become a new pre-workout ritual? Scientists say more research is needed, but it's a fascinating first step.
why_it_matters: This is a case study in how science news works: a small, single-session experiment can make exciting headlines long before the effect is confirmed, so noticing sample size and missing measurements is a real skill for anyone reading health or fitness claims.

background_read: Smell is the only sense that goes almost straight to the parts of the brain that handle memory and emotion, which is why one scent can suddenly remind you of a place or a meal.

The new study comes from the University of Malaya (a research university in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia) and was published in Frontiers in Physiology (a peer-reviewed science journal about how the body works).

Earlier sports research has tested smells like peppermint or ammonia during exercise to see whether they change how hard a workout feels, so this is part of a longer line of experiments on the senses and performance.

Small single-session experiments like this one — 23 participants, one visit — are common in exercise science because they are cheap and quick, but their results often shrink or vanish when repeated with larger, more varied groups.
There is also the well-known placebo effect: if you expect something to help you, your body may really perform better, which is why scientists compare against a control such as water.

perspectives.description: A pleasant smell is free, harmless, and easy to try before a workout. If it even slightly lowers how hard training feels, gym-goers may get more reps and better sessions. It also supports the growing view that the brain and body are one system, not separate.

Only 23 moderately trained men were tested, and no hormones or brain activity were measured, so the biological story is a guess. The results may not repeat in larger studies or apply to women, older adults, or beginners. Sniffing chocolate is not a proven training method yet.

Sports and nutrition science has a long history of small studies that look dramatic and then fail to replicate. Expectation and placebo effects are extremely hard to separate from a real scent effect, and a control of water helps but does not fully solve that problem.

Future work could measure hormones and brain activity, use bigger and more diverse groups, and test other food smells. If the effect holds up, pre-workout aroma rituals — or even scented gym products — could become a real, low-cost tool.
